Since a walk satisfying the conditions of $\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}$ hits level $L^-$ at a non-truncated edge, and it does not backtrack from level $L^-$ to level $L^--M$, we can bound the required probability by the probability of $Z^{(1)}$ hitting level $L^-$ at a non-truncated descendant of $f$. There are $\le (e^{C_{\mathrm{vol}} R}d_{\mathrm{max}})^{M+1}\le e^{C(\log\log N)^2}$ non-truncated descendants of $f$ at level $L^-$ (where $C$ is a large constant), and by the definition of $\mathrm{Tr}'\left(\cdot\right)$ the probability of hitting level $L^-$ at a specific one of them is $\le\frac{1}{\sqrt N}e^{-\sqrt{\log N}}$. This gives the required bound.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{bound_num_explored_num_bad}
For all sufficiently large values of $n$, the total number of vertices explored during the explorations from $z_1$, ..., $z_{L_x+L_y}$ is
\[
\le\quad N^{\frac12\left(1+c_L^+\right)}\exp\left(2A\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{V}\log N}{\mathfrak{h}}}\right).
\]
Also, there exists a positive constant~$C$ (not depending on $\widehat{T}_{x,K}$ and $\widehat{T}_{y,K}$) so that the number $\rm{Bad}$ of bad vertices $z_i$ satisfies
\[
\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\rm{Bad}\ge C\;\middle\vert\;\left\{\widehat{T}^a_{x,K},\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}\right)\quad=\quad o\left(\frac{1}{N^2}\right).
\]
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By the definition of $\mathrm{Tr}\left(\cdot,A\right)$, the number of vertices at each level of a given tree $T(z_i)$ that are not truncated due to the truncation criterion $\mathrm{Tr}\left(\cdot,A\right)$ is $\le N^{\frac12(1+c_L^+)}\exp\left(A\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{V}\log N}{\mathfrak{h}}}\right)e^{C_{\mathrm{vol}} 2R}$. The number of levels is $\asymp\log N$ and the number of $z_i$ is $\le e^{C_{\mathrm{vol}} 2R{(K+1)}}{d_{\mathrm{max}}^{(K+1)}}\le e^{\mathrm{const}\cdot(\log\log N)^2}$. (Here $C_{\mathrm{vol}}$ is the constant from \Cref{def:atypical_ball}\eqref{item:large_vol}.) Using that $\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{V}\log N}{\mathfrak{h}}}\gg(\log\log N)^2$ we get the bound on the number of explored vertices.

In a random quasi-tree, the probability of the new endpoint of a newly revealed long-range edge taking any specific value is $\le\max_{x,y}p^{\mathrm{red}}_{x,y}\lesssim\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}$. Hence each time we reveal a new $(R+R)$-ball, the probability that it intersects the $(R+R)$-ball of some  $z_i$ is $\le\frac{e^{C_{\mathrm{vol}}2R(K+1)}d_{\mathrm{max}}^{K+1}e^{C_{\mathrm{vol}} 4R}}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}\le \frac{e^{\mathrm{const}( \log\log N)^2}}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}$. The probability that it happens at least $C$ times is at most
\[
\exp\left(C\left(\frac12\left(1+c_L^+\right)\log N+2A\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{V}\log N}{\mathfrak{h}}}+\mathrm{const} (\log \log N)^2-(1-\beta)\log N-\log\log N\right)\right).
\]
For sufficiently small $c_L^+$ such that $\frac12\left(1+c_L^+\right)<(1-\beta)$ and for sufficiently large $C$ this is $o\left(\frac{1}{N^2}\right)$. The inequality $\frac12\left(1+c_L^+\right)<(1-\beta)$ is true for sufficiently small  $c_L^+$, as long as $\beta<\frac12$. We note that this is the only place where a nontrivial constraint on the value of $\beta$ appears.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{Succ_i_prob_on_Tzi}
For any constant $\theta\in(0,1)$ the following holds. Let $i\in\{1,2,...,L_x\}$ and let $Z$ be a simple random walk on $T_x(z_i)$ starting from $z_i$. Let $\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}^{T(z_i)}$ denote the event that $Z$ satisfies (iii)-(vii) from the definition of $\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}$ in \Cref{sec:coupling}. Then we have
\[
\mathbb{P}_{z_i}\!\left(\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}^{T(z_i)}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{i-1}\right)\quad\ge\quad(1-\theta)\1{\{z_i\text{ good}\}}.
\]
An analogous bound holds for $i\in\{L_x+1,...,L_x+L_y\}$ and a walk on $T_y(z_i)$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The proof is similar to the proof of~\cite[Lemma 5.6]{random_matching}. Let us work on the event that $z_i$ is good.

Firstly, we show that the probability of $\left\{\Omega_{\mathrm{typ}}\left(\tau_{L^+}\right),\Omega_{\partial}\left(\tau_{L^+}\right),\tau_{L^+}\le\frac{2}{\nu}L^+\right\}=:\mathcal{A}$ can be lower bounded by a constant arbitrarily close to 1.
\begin{itemize}
\item By \Cref{speed_concentration} we can bound $\mathbb{P}\!\left(\tau_{L^+}>\frac{2}{\nu}L^+,\:\Omega_{\mathrm{typ}}\left(\sigma_{L^+}\right),\:\Omega_{\partial}\left(\sigma_{L^+}\right)\right)$ by an arbitrarily small constant.
\item Using \Cref{bound_sigma1} and that by \Cref{iid_decomp} we have $\sigma_{k}\wedge\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}\wedge\tau_{\partial}\le_{\mathrm{st}}\sum_{j=1}^{k}s_j$ where $s_j$ are independent, $s_1\stackrel{\mathrm{d}}{=}\sigma_{1}\wedge\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}\wedge\tau_{\partial}$, and $s_j\stackrel{\mathrm{d}}{=}\sigma'_{1}\wedge\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}'\wedge\tau_{\partial}'$ for $j\ge2$, we get that\\
$\mathbb{P}\!\left(\sigma_{L^+}>(\log N)^{3/2},\:\Omega_{\mathrm{typ}}\left((\log N)^{3/2}\right),\:\Omega_{\partial}\left((\log N)^{3/2}\right)\right)\ll1$.
\item From \Cref{bound_atyp_prob} we know that for each newly sampled $(R+R)$-ball, the probability that it is atypical is $\lesssim\left(\frac{1}{\log N}\right)^2$. Hence the probability of any of the first $(\log N)^{3/2}$ different balls visited by $Z$ being atypical is $o(1)$, therefore $\mathbb{P}\!\left(\Omega_{\mathrm{typ}}\left((\log N)^{3/2}\right)^c\right)\ll1$.
\item By \eqref{item:hit_boundary} in the definition of atypical balls (\Cref{def:atypical_ball}) we know that starting a walk in a typical ball, the probability that it visits at least $R$ vertices in a ball before $\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}$ is $\le\left(\frac{1}{\log N}\right)^2$. Hence $\mathbb{P}\!\left(\Omega_{\partial}\left((\log N)^{3/2}\right)^c,\:\Omega_{\mathrm{typ}}\left((\log N)^{3/2}\right)\right)\ll1$.
\end{itemize}
Combining these, we can upper bound $\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathcal{A}^c\right)$ by an arbitrarily small constant.

Now we bound the probability that the event $\mathcal{A}$ holds, but $Z$ crosses a truncated edge by time~$\tau_{L^+}$.
\begin{itemize}
\item By \Cref{bound_trunc_prob} and \Cref{bound_truncprime_prob} we can bound the probability that $\mathcal{A}$ holds but $Z$ crosses an edge satisfying $\mathrm{Tr}\left(\cdot,A\right)$ or $\mathrm{Tr}'\left(\cdot\right)$ by level $L^+$ by an arbitrarily small constant.
\item Let us consider a vertex $v$ in $T_x(z_i)$ that is the newly revealed endpoint of a long-range edge and whose $(R+R)$-ball we are just about to reveal. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be the set of already explored vertices. Then we can explore the ball of $v$ as follows. Consider $v$ and for each $w$ in $G$ let us sample whether $v\sim_{\mathrm{g}} w$ holds in $T_x(z_i)$ and in $G^*$, using the appropriate distribution in each graph, coupled via the optimal coupling. If $v\not\sim_{\mathrm{g}} w$ for all $w\in\mathcal{D}$ then the optimal coupling is successful. Then consider the green and black neighbours of $v$ one by one, and for each of these vertices and each $w$ in $G$ sample whether there is a green edge between them. Continue similarly, until the whole of the $(R+R)$-ball is revealed or until one of the couplings fails. Note that on the event that the $(R+R)$-ball in $G$ does not intersect $\mathcal{D}$, the coupling is successful.
\item Similarly, we can see that given an $(R+R)$-ball in $T_x(z_i)$, where we are just about to reveal the red degrees, the probability that the optimal coupling of these red degrees in $T_x(z_i)$ and $G^*$ fails is bounded by the probability that there is a red edge in $G^*$ leading from the ball to the set $\mathcal{D}$ of already explored vertices.
\item Now consider a vertex $v$ in $T_x(z_i)$ and a long-range half-edge from it whose other endpoint we are just about to reveal. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be the set of already revealed vertices. By the above, the probability that the long-range edge gets truncated due to the optimal coupling of the endpoint failing, due to the optimal coupling of the ball around the other endpoint failing, or due to the ball around the other endpoint containing an already revealed vertex can be bounded by the probability that a randomly sampled red edge from $v$ leads to a vertex that is in $\mathcal{D}$ or within distance $2R$ from $\mathcal{D}$ in $G^*$.
\item The probability of a red edge leading to any specific vertex is $\lesssim\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}$. From \Cref{bound_num_explored_num_bad} we know that $|\mathcal{D}|\le N^{\frac12\left(1+c_L^+\right)}\exp\left(2A\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{V}\log N}{\mathfrak{h}}}\right)$. From \Cref{volume_high_prob_bound} we know that whp any ball of radius $2R$ in $G^*$ has volume $\lesssim e^{CR}$ where $C$ is a positive constant. So the probability of a newly revealed long-range edge getting truncated due to an overlap or due to the optimal coupling failing is $\lesssim N^{\frac12\left(1+c_L^+\right)}\exp\left(2A\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{V}\log N}{\mathfrak{h}}}\right)\exp\left(CC_R\log\log N\right)\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}\log N$, where the final $\log N$ term comes from \Cref{cond_green_red_deg} and from the fact that whp all vertices in our random graph have degree $\le \log N$. Hence, the probability that the walk $Z$ up to time $\frac{2}{\nu}L^+$ crosses a long-range edge that is truncated, and the first such edge is truncated due to an overlap or due to the optimal coupling failing, is $o(1)$. 
\end{itemize}
This bounds the probability that \eqref{item:Lplus_without_crossing_truncated} fails while \eqref{item:Omegabound_holds} and \eqref{item:tauLplus_bound} hold.

Finally, we can bound the probability of \eqref{item:not_backtrack_from_Lminus} or \eqref{item:enough_small_degrees} failing as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item The probability of $Z$ backtracking $M$ levels from level $L^-$ is $\le(1-p_{\mathrm{esc}})^M\ll1$.
\item Every time a new $(R+R)$-ball is revealed, its centre has $d_{\mathrm{rg}}(\cdot)$ distributed as $d_{\mathrm{rg}}$, independently of everything else revealed before. From \Cref{degree_exp_moment} we know that this has a bounded expectation and variance. For each level between $L^-$ and $L^+$, consider the first vertex at that level visited by the walk. Their $d_{\mathrm{rg}}(\cdot)$ degrees are independent with the above distribution, so for a sufficiently large constant $C_{\mathrm{deg}}$, with probability $1-o(1)$, at least half of them have $d_{\mathrm{rg}}(\cdot)\leC_{\mathrm{deg}}$. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{Succ_i_prob}
There exists $\theta\in(0,1)$ such that the following holds. Let $i\in\{1,2,...,L_x\}$ and let $Z$ be a simple random walk on $T_x$ starting from $z_i$. Let $\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}^{i}$ denote the event that $Z$ satisfies (ii)-(vii) from the definition of $\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}$ in \Cref{sec:coupling}. Then we have
\[
\mathbb{P}_{z_i}\!\left(\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}^i\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{i-1}\right)\quad\ge\quad\theta\1{\{z_i\text{ good}\}}.
\]
An analogous bound holds for $i\in\{L_x+1,...,L_x+L_y\}$ and a walk on $T_y$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
We can couple $Z$ to a walk on $T_x(z_i)$ started from $z_i$ such that on the event that $Z$ does not visit level $(K-1)$ up to time $\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}\wedge\tau_{L^+}$, the two walks agree up to $\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}\wedge\tau_{L^+}$.

By \Cref{transience_until_nonbinary} this event has probability at least $p_{\mathrm{esc}}$. Then use \Cref{Succ_i_prob_on_Tzi} for the walk on $T_x(z_i)$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{Succhat_i_prob}
There exists $\theta\in(0,1)$ such that the following holds. Let $i\in\{1,2,...,L_x\}$ and let $Z$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}^i$ be defined as in \Cref{Succ_i_prob}. Let $\widehat{Z}$ be a simple random walk on $\widehat{T}_x$ starting from $z_i$, defined up to the first time it hits level $L^+$ or crosses a blue half-edge, coupled to $Z$ such that they agree up to this time. Let $\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}^{i}$ denote the event that $\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}^i$ holds and $Z$ and $\widehat{Z}$ satisfy (iii)-(v) from the definition of $\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}$ in \Cref{sec:coupling}. Then we have
\[
\mathbb{P}_{z_i}\!\left(\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}^i\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{i-1}\right)\quad\ge\quad\theta\1{\{z_i\text{ good}\}}.
\]
An analogous bound holds for $i\in\{L_x+1,...,L_x+L_y\}$ and a walk on $\widehat{T}_y$.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Let us work on the event that $z_i$ is good. From \Cref{Succ_i_prob} we know that $\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}^i$ holds with positive probability. In what follows let us condition on $(Z_t)_{t\le\tau_{L^+}}$ and work on the event that it satisfies $\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}^i$.

Firstly, we bound the probability that \eqref{item:no_bluetrunc_before_Lplus} in the definition of $\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}$ fails.

Let us consider a vertex $v$ whose blue degree we are just about to reveal. If the set of vertices with already revealed blue degrees is denoted by $\mathcal{D}$, then the probability that the optimal coupling for the blue degree of $v$ fails can be bounded as $\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathrm{Bin}\!\left(\log N\sum_{v\in D}d_{\mathrm{b}}(v),p^{\mathrm{blue}}\right)>0\right)\le\frac{|\mathcal{D}|}{N\log N}(\log N)^2$ using \Cref{cond_green_red_deg} and that with high probability the graph does not have any vertex with degree greater than $\log N$. 

Using that by \Cref{bound_num_explored_num_bad} the overall number of explored vertices is $\le N^{\frac12(1+c_L^++o(1))}$ and that by definition a typical ball has volume $\le e^{C_{\mathrm{vol}} C_R\log\log N}$, we get that the probability of a given long-range edge leading to a typical ball, but being blue-truncated is $\ll\frac{1}{N^{\mathrm{const}}}$. If we condition on $(Z_t)_{t\le\tau_{L^+}}$ and work on the event that it satisfies $\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}^i$, and we reveal the blue degrees in the balls as they are first visited by $Z$, we get that the probability of $(Z_t)_{t\le\tau_{L^+}}$ crossing a blue-truncated long-range edge is $\ll\frac{1}{\nu}L^+\frac{1}{\log N}\asymp1$.

Now we turn to lower bounding the probability that \eqref{item:no_blue_between_K_Lminus} in the definition of $\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}$ holds.

By assumption the walk $(Z_t)_{t\le\tau_{L^+}}$ visits $\le\frac{2}{\nu}L^+\asymp\log N$ vertices before level $L^-$, counted with multiplicity. Denote the set of these vertices by $\mathcal{S}$. Let $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{many}}$ be the set of vertices before  level $L^-$ that $(Z_t)_{t\le\tau_{L^+}}$ visits $\ge C$ times. Then $|\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{many}}|\le\frac{\frac{2}{\nu}L^+}{C}$. The sum of the blue degrees of these vertices in $\widehat{T}$ is $\le_{\mathrm{st}}\mathrm{Bin}\!\left(N|\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{many}}|,p^{\mathrm{blue}}\right)$, where $p^{\mathrm{blue}}\asymp\frac{1}{N\log N}$. Hence the probability of any vertex in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{many}}$ having at least one blue half-edge tends to 0 as $C\to\infty$.

The sum over vertices in $\mathcal{S}$ of the blue degrees in $\widehat{T}$ is $\le_{\mathrm{st}}\mathrm{Bin}\!\left(N\frac{2}{\nu}L^+,p^{\mathrm{blue}}\right)$, hence the probability that this is $\ge C$ tends to 0 as $C\to\infty$.

So with positive probability there is no blue half-edge from the set $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{many}}$ and the total number of blue half-edges from $\mathcal{S}$ is $\le C$. On this event, the probability that $(\widehat{Z}_t)_{t\le\tau_{L^+}}$ does not cross a blue half-edge below level $L^-$ is bounded away from 0.

Finally, we lower bound the probability that \eqref{item:blue_between_Lminus_Lplus} in the definition of $\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}$ holds.

By the definition of $\Omega_{\mathrm{succ}}^i$ we know that at least $\frac12(L^+-L^-)\asymp\log N$ vertices visited by $Z$ between levels $L^-$ and $L^+$ have $d_{\mathrm{rg}}(\cdot)\leC_{\mathrm{deg}}$. For a given vertex $v$ we have $\mathbb{P}\!\left(d_{\mathrm{b}}(v)>0\right)\asymp\frac{1}{\log N}$, so with positive probability at least one of the above vertices has at least one blue half-edge. On this event the probability of $(\widehat{Z}_t)_{t\le\tau_{L^+}}$ crossing a blue half-edge between levels $L^-$ and $L^+$ is bounded away from 0.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The proof uses a martingale argument similar to the one in the proof of \cite[Proposition 5.7]{random_matching}.

Conditional on $\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{L_x+L_y}$, the walks $\widehat{Z}^{(1)}$ and $\widehat{Z}^{(2)}$ are independent, so it is sufficient to prove that for some positive constant $\theta$ we have
\begin{align}\label{eq:Succhat_prob_one_walk}
\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\widehat{Z}^{(j)}\text{ satisfies the conditions of } \widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{L_x+L_y}\right)>\theta\;\middle\vert\;\left\{\widehat{T}^a_{x,K},\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}\right)\quad\ge\quad1-o\left(\frac{1}{N^2}\right)
\end{align}
for $j=1,2$. We present the proof for $\widehat{Z}^{(1)}$ below, the proof for $\widehat{Z}^{(2)}$ follows analogously.

For each $i\in\{1,2,...,L_x\}$ let $h(z_i)=\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(\widehat{Z}^{(1)}_{\tau_K}=z_i,\:\tau_K<\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}\wedge\tau_{\partial}\wedge\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\wedge\tau_{\rho^a}\;\middle\vert\;\left\{\widehat{T}^a_{x,K},\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}\right)$. \footnote{Recall that $\tau_{\partial}$ denotes the first time that the walk visits the $R$th different vertex in an $(R+R)$-ball, i.e.\ the first time that $\Omega_{\partial}\left(\cdot\right)$ fails.} Let
\begin{align*}
\widehat{V}:=\quad\left\{z_i:\:i\in\{1,...,L_x\},\:\mathbb{P}_{z_i}\!\left(\left(\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}^i\right)^c\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{L_x+L_y}\right)\ge1-\theta_1\right\},
\end{align*}
where $\theta_1\in(0,1)$ is a constant that is smaller than the constant in \Cref{Succhat_i_prob}.

We will prove that
\begin{align}\label{eq:bound_hVhat}
\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(h\left(\widehat{V}\right)\ge\theta_4+(1-\theta_5)\sum_{i=1}^{L_x}h(z_i)\;\middle\vert\;\left\{\widehat{T}^a_{x,K},\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}\right)\quad\ll\quad\frac{1}{N^2},
\end{align}
for some given constant $\theta_5\in(0,1)$ and any constant $\theta_4\in(0,1)$.

Once we have this, we can conclude the proof of \eqref{eq:Succhat_prob_one_walk} as follows. Note that
\begin{align*}
&\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\widehat{Z}^{(1)}\text{ fails the conditions of }\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{L_x+L_y}\right)\\
&\le\quad\left(1-\sum_{i}h(z_i)\right)+ \sum_{z_i\in\widehat{V}}h(z_i)\mathbb{P}_{z_i}\!\left(\left(\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}^i\right)^c\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{L_x+L_y}\right) +\sum_{z_i\not\in\widehat{V}}h(z_i)\mathbb{P}_{z_i}\!\left(\left(\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}^i\right)^c\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{L_x+L_y}\right)\\
&\le\quad \left(1-\sum_{i}h(z_i)\right)+h\left(\widehat{V}\right)+h\left(\widehat{V}^c\right)(1-\theta_1)\quad =\quad1-h\left(\widehat{V}^c\right)\theta_1.
\end{align*}

By \eqref{eq:bound_hVhat}, with probability $1-o\left(\frac{1}{N^2}\right)$ we have
\begin{align*}
1-h\left(\widehat{V}^c\right)\quad=\quad\left(1-\sum_{i}h(z_i)\right)+h\left(\widehat{V}\right)\quad\le\quad \left(1-\sum_{i}h(z_i)\right)+\theta_4+(1-\theta_5)\sum_{i}h(z_i)&\\
\le\quad1+\theta_4-\theta_5\sum_{i}h(z_i)\quad\le\quad1+\theta_4-\theta_5c_{\mathrm{nice}}'\:,&
\end{align*}
where in the last $\le$ we used \Cref{niceprime_hit_level_K}. Choosing $\theta_4$ sufficiently small we can make $1+\theta_4-\theta_5c_{\mathrm{nice}}'$ bounded away from 1, hence making $1-h\left(\widehat{V}^c\right)\theta_1$ bounded away from 1. This finishes the proof of \eqref{eq:Succhat_prob_one_walk}.

Now we present the proof of \eqref{eq:bound_hVhat}.

By \Cref{bound_num_explored_num_bad} with probability $1-o\left(\frac{1}{N^2}\right)$ we have $\#\left\{i:\:z_i\text{ bad}\right\}\lesssim1$. Also, by \Cref{transience_until_nonbinary} we have $h(z_i)\le(1-p_{\mathrm{esc}})^K\ll1$ for each $i$. So it remains to bound $\sum_{i}h(z_i)\1{z_i\in\widehat{V}}\1{\left\{z_i\text{ good}\right\}}$.

Using \Cref{Succhat_i_prob} and Markov's inequality, we get that
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\!\left[h(z_i)\1{\{z_i\in\widehat{V}\}}\1{\{z_i\text{ good}\}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{i-1}\right]\quad=\quad h(z_i)\1{\{z_i\text{ good}\}}\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}_{z_i}\!\left(\left(\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}^i\right)^c\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{L_x+L_y}\right)\ge1-\theta_1\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{i-1}\right)\\
\le\quad h(z_i)\1{\{z_i\text{ good}\}}\frac{1-\theta_3}{1-\theta_1},
\end{align*}
where $\theta_3\in(0,1)$ is the constant from \Cref{Succhat_i_prob}. We chose $\theta_1<\theta_3$, hence $\frac{1-\theta_3}{1-\theta_1}<1$.

Let
\[
R_i:=\quad h(z_i)\1{\{z_i\in\widehat{V}\}}\1{\{z_i\text{ good}\}},\qquad M_k:=\quad\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left(R_i-\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_i\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{i-1}\right]\right).
\]
Then $(M_k)$ is a martingale with respect to $\left(\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{k}\right)$, and $|M_k-M_{k-1}|\le h(z_k)$. Also \[
M_{L_x}\quad\ge\quad\sum_{i}R_i-\frac{1-\theta_3}{1-\theta_1}\sum_ih(z_i).
\]


Then using the Azuma-Hoeffding inequality and that $h(z_i)\le(1-p_{\mathrm{esc}})^K$ for all $i$, we get that for sufficiently large values of $C_K$, for any $\theta_4>0$ we have
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\sum_{i}h(z_i)\1{\{z_i\in\widehat{V}\}}\1{\{z_i\text{ good}\}}>\theta_4+\frac{1-\theta_3}{1-\theta_1}\sum_ih(z_i)\;\middle\vert\;\left\{\widehat{T}^a_{x,K},\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}\right)\quad\le\quad\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(M_{L_x}>\theta_4\;\middle\vert\;\left\{\widehat{T}^a_{x,K},\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}\right)&\\
\le\quad\exp\left(-\frac{c\theta_4^2}{\sum_{i}h(z_i)^2}\right)\quad\le\quad\exp\left(-c\theta_4^2(\log N)^2\right)\quad\ll\quad\frac{1}{N^2}.&
\end{align*}

This finishes the proof of \eqref{eq:bound_hVhat} with $\theta_5=1-\frac{1-\theta_3}{1-\theta_1}$, hence finishing the proof of \Cref{Succhat_prob}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
We can write
\begin{align*}
&\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}^{(2)}-1}=y,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}^{(2)}\le C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right)\quad\\
&\ge\quad\sum_{z}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=z,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right) \mathbb{P}_{z}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}-1}=y,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right)\\
&=\quad\sum_{z}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=z,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right) \mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}-1}=z,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right)\frac{d_{\mathrm{b}}(y)}{d_{\mathrm{b}}(z)}\\
&=\quadd_{\mathrm{b}}(y)\sum_{w,z}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}-1}=w,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right) \frac{1}{d_{\mathrm{b}}(w)}\\
&\hspace{6cm}\cdot\mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}-1}=z,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right) \frac{1}{d_{\mathrm{b}}(z)}\1{z\sim_{\mathrm{b}} w}\\
&=\quadd_{\mathrm{b}}(y)\sum_{e,f}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right) \mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right)\1{e\sim_{\mathrm{b}} f}
\end{align*}
where the last sum is taken over blue half-edges, $X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e$ means that the first blue half-edge crossed by $X$ is $e$, and $e\sim_{\mathrm{b}} f$ means that $e$ and $f$ are the two ends of the same blue edge.

Let $x$ and $y$ be two vertices of $G$ and let $\left\{\widehat{T}_{x,K}^a,\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}$ denote the event that $x$ is almost nice, with distinguished edge $\{x,x^a\}$, $y$ is nice, the level $K$ neighbourhood of $x$ in $G^*\setminus\left\{\{x,x^a\}\right\}$ and the level $K$ neighbourhood of $y$ in $G^*$ are disjoint and do not contain $x^a$, and these neighbourhoods look like $\widehat{T}_{x,K}$ and $\widehat{T}_{y,K}$ respectively.

Let us consider the explorations and couplings defined in \Cref{sec:coupling}, and let us abbreviate $\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{L_x+L_y}$ as $\widehat{\mathcal{F}}$. Let $\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b$ denote the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\widehat{\mathcal{F}}$ and all the blue degrees in $G^*$. Let $A$ denote the high probability event of \Cref{blue_almost_unif} for the blue degrees $(d_{\mathrm{b}}(v))$ in $G^*$.

Then we can write the following.
\begin{align*}
&\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}^{(2)}-1}=y,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}^{(2)}\le C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right)\:<\:c\frac{\log{N}}{N}d_{\mathrm{b}}(y),\: A\;\middle\vert\;\left\{\widehat{T}_{x,K}^a,\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}\right)\\
&\le \quad\mathbb{P}\Bigg(\sum_{e,f}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right)\\
&\hspace{3cm}\cdot\mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;G^*\right)\1{e\sim_{\mathrm{b}} f}\:<\:c\frac{\log{N}}{N},\: A\:\Bigg|\:\left\{\widehat{T}_{x,K}^a,\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}\Bigg)\\
&\le\quad\mathbb{P}\Bigg(\sum_{e,f}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}<\tau_{x^a}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)\\
&\hspace{3cm}\cdot\mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)\1{e\sim_{\mathrm{b}} f}\:<\:c\frac{\log{N}}{N},\: A\:\Bigg|\:\left\{\widehat{T}_{x,K}^a,\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}\Bigg)\\
&\le\quad\mathbb{P}\Bigg(\sum_{e,f}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}<\tau_{x^a}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)\\
&\hspace{3cm}\mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)\1{e\sim_{\mathrm{b}} f} \:<\:c\frac{\log{N}}{N},\\ &\hspace{4cm}\:\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)>\theta,\:\sum_{v}d_{\mathrm{b}}(v)<C_{\mathrm{blue}}\frac{N}{\log N},\: A \:\Bigg|\:\left\{\widehat{T}_{x,K}^a,\widehat{T}_{y,K}\right\}\Bigg) +o\left(\frac{1}{N^2}\right).
\end{align*}

In the last line, $C_{\mathrm{blue}}$ is a sufficiently large positive constant, $\theta$ is a sufficiently small positive constant, and we used \Cref{Succhat_prob} and \Cref{total_blue_degree}.
Now let us fix $\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b$ such that $\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)>\theta$, $\sum_{v}d_{\mathrm{b}}(v)<C_{\mathrm{blue}}\frac{N}{\log N}$, and $A$ holds. Then assuming that $C>\frac{8}{\nu}c_L$ and using the notation from \Cref{sec:coupling} we can write
\begin{align*}
&\sum_{e,f}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N,\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}<\tau_{x^a}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right) \mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\le  \frac12C\log N\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)\1{e\sim_{\mathrm{b}} f}\quad\\
&\quad\ge\quad\sum_{e,f}\mathbb{P}_{x,y}\!\left(\widehat{X}^{(1)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\:\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}<\tau_{x^a},\:\widehat{X}^{(2)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\:\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)\1{e\sim_{\mathrm{b}} f}\\
&\quad=\quad\sum_{e,f}\mathbb{P}_{x,y}\!\left(\widehat{Z}^{(1)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\:\widehat{Z}^{(2)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\:\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)\1{e\sim_{\mathrm{b}} f}\:.
\end{align*}
Let $\mathcal{I}$ denote the set of blue half-edges. By assumption we know that $|\mathcal{I}|\leC_{\mathrm{blue}}\frac{N}{\log N}$ and $\sum_{e,f}\mathbb{P}_{x,y}\!\left(\widehat{Z}^{(1)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\:\widehat{Z}^{(2)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\:\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)=\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)>\theta$, and from \Cref{bound_prob_specific_blue_edge} we also know that $\mathbb{P}_{x,y}\!\left(\widehat{Z}^{(1)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\:\widehat{Z}^{(2)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\:\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)\le\frac{1}{N\log N}$ for each pair $(e,f)$.

Using \cite[Lemma 5.1]{cutoff_NBRW_on_sparse_random_graphs} with weights $w_{e,f}=\mathbb{P}_{x,y}\!\left(\widehat{Z}^{(1)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\:\widehat{Z}^{(2)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\:\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)$, and using that by \Cref{blue_almost_unif} on event $A$ the matching of the blue half-edges is distributed as a uniform random matching of $\mathcal{I}$ conditioned on a high probability event, we get that for sufficiently small values of $c$ we have
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\sum_{e,f}\mathbb{P}_{x,y}\!\left(\widehat{Z}^{(1)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=e,\:\widehat{Z}^{(2)}_{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}}=f,\:\widehat{\Omega}_{\mathrm{succ}}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)\1{e\sim_{\mathrm{b}} f}\:<\:c\frac{\log N}{N}\;\middle\vert\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_b\right)\quad\ll\quad\frac{1}{N^2}.
\end{align*}
This finishes the proof using the union bound.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{hit_almost_nice_quickly}
For any $\theta\in(0,1)$ there exists $C>0$ such that whp $G^*$ satisfies the following. For any vertex $x$, with probability at least $\theta$, a simple random walk on $G^*$ starting from $x$ hits $V'_{\mathrm{nice}}$ by time $C\log N$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{nice:stopped_walk_transience}
There exists a positive constant $q_{\mathrm{esc}}$ (not depending on any of the parameters, nor on the dimension $d$) with the following property.

For any realisation $T$ of a random quasi-tree, and any vertex $x$ of $T$, the probability that a walk from $x$ does not return to $x$ without first hitting the boundary of a ball can be lower bounded as
\[
\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(\tau_x^+>\tau_{\partial}\right)\quad\ge\quad\frac{q_{\mathrm{esc}}}{\deg_T(x)},
\]
while for any long-range edge $e$, the probability that a walk from $x$ does not cross $e$ without hitting a boundary first can be lower bounded as
\[
\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(\tau_e>\tau_{\partial}\right)\quad\ge\quadq_{\mathrm{esc}}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{def:thetaT}
Consider a quasi-tree $T$ and let $e$ be a long-range edge. Let $\ell$ be the level of $e$ and for $i\in\{1,2,...,\ell\}$ let $e_i$ be the long-range edge that is the level $i$ ancestor of $e$. Then let us consider a graph that consists of the balls containing $e_i^-$ for each $i$, the long-range half-edges from these balls, and the long-range edges $(e_i)_i$. Let us consider a walk on this graph started from $\rho$ that takes steps like a simple random walk, except for the following. It is not allowed to cross from $e_i^+$ to~$e_i^-$ for all $i\leq \ell$. If it crosses a long-range half-edge\footnote{Note that $(e_i)$ are not considered as half-edges.}, with probability $q_{\mathrm{esc}}$ it gets terminated, otherwise, it crosses back and continues walking. It is also terminated if it hits the boundary of a ball or it hits $e^+$. Let $\theta_T(e)$ denote the probability that this walk reaches $e^+$ without getting terminated for some other reason first. Here $q_{\mathrm{esc}}$ denotes the constant from \Cref{nice:stopped_walk_transience}.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
\label{def:trunc_nice}
Given a quasi-tree $T$ with root $\rho$, and a long-range edge $e$ in $T$, let us say that $e$ is \emph{truncated} if $\theta_{T}(e)\le\frac{c_{\mathrm{trunc}}}{\log N}$, where $c_{\mathrm{trunc}}$ is a positive constant to be chosen later.
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
\label{def:nbhd_for_hitting_nice}
Consider a random quasi-tree $T$ rooted at a given vertex $x$. Let us reveal the ball around $x$, together with the long-range half-edges from it, and see which of the long-range half-edges (if any) are truncated according to \Cref{def:trunc_nice}. Then in $G^*$ reveal the ball of radius $R$ around $x$ according to the green and black edges, and couple it exactly to the ball around the root of $T$. Also reveal the red and blue degrees of each vertex in this ball in $G^*$ and couple them exactly to the corresponding red and blue degrees in $T$. (The two balls and the red and blue degrees of their vertices have the exact same distribution, so they can be coupled so that they always agree.)

One by one, consider the long-range half-edges from the revealed ball in $T$. If a long-range half-edge is truncated, then we also truncate it in $G^*$ and do not explore further in that direction. Otherwise, we reveal the ball in $T$ around its other endpoint, and we also reveal the red and blue degrees from this ball. We also reveal the other endpoint of the corresponding long-range edge in $G^*$, the ball of radius $R$ around it according to the green and black degrees, and the red and blue degrees of each vertex in the ball, coupling all these to the ball in $T$ using the optimal coupling. If the new ball in $T$ contains any of the previously revealed vertices or the optimal coupling fails, we do the following. In case this is the first time it happens, we denote the long-range edge leading to the new ball by $\widetilde{e}$ and truncate it, not exploring further in this direction. If it is not the first time this happens, then we declare the exploration unsuccessful and terminate the process.

Once we considered all the long-range half-edges from the ball around $x$, we continue similarly with the long-range half-edges from the level 1 balls, and then continue similarly level by level (until we need to terminate the exploration and declare it unsuccessful, or until we successfully couple a certain subgraph of $G^*$ with all the balls of $T$ that can be reached from the root without crossing a truncated edge or $\widetilde{e}$.)

If the exploration was successful, let $A$ denote the set of truncated long-range half-edges in $T$, except for~$\widetilde{e}$.
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{nice:coupling_success_and_nbhd_size}
Fix a vertex $x$ in $G$. With probability $1-o\left(\frac1N\right)$ the exploration described in \Cref{def:nbhd_for_hitting_nice} succeeds, and the explored random neighbourhood has size $\le N^c$ where $c>0$ is a constant that can be made arbitrarily small by choosing $c_R$ sufficiently small.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{nice:nbhd_properties}
For any constant $\theta\in(0,1)$ there exist positive constants $C$ and $C'$ with the following property.
For any fixed vertex $x$ in $G$, with probability $1-o\left(\frac1N\right)$ the exploration described in \Cref{def:nbhd_for_hitting_nice} succeeds and a walk $X$ on $T$ from $x$ satisfies the following.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item\label{item:nice:bound_num_visited} With high probability the walk $X$ visits $\le C'\log N$ different vertices by the time it hits $A\cup\{\widetilde{e}\}$.
\item\label{item:nice:bound_time} With probability at least $1-\theta$ the number of steps it takes for the walk $X$ to visit $C'\log N$ different vertices or hit $A\cup\{\widetilde{e}\}\cup\partial$ is $\le C\log N$.
\item\label{item:nice:not_hit_etil} With probability at least $q_{\mathrm{esc}}$ the walk $X$ hits $A\cup\partial$ before hitting $\widetilde{e}$. (Here $q_{\mathrm{esc}}$ is the constant from \Cref{nice:stopped_walk_transience}, and it does not depend on any other parameter.)
\item\label{item:nice:bound_prob_given_e} For each $e\in A$ the probability of $X$ hitting $A\cup\{\widetilde{e}\}\cup\partial$ at $e$ is $\le\frac{c_{\mathrm{trunc}}}{\log N}$.
\item\label{item:nice:not_hit_boundary} {With high probability the walk $X$ hits $A\cup\{\widetilde{e}\}$ before hitting $\partial$.}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{nice:thetaT_properties} For any realisation of $T$, the function $\theta_T$ defined in \Cref{def:thetaT} satisfies the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item\label{item:thetaT_multiplicative} For $(e_i)_{i=1}^{\ell}$ as in \Cref{def:thetaT} and $e_0^+=\rho$, we have $\theta_T(e)=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}\theta_{T(e_{i-1}^+)}(e_i)$.
\item\label{item:thetaT_exp_decay} $\theta_T(e)\le(1-q_{\mathrm{esc}})^{\ell(e)}$.
\item\label{item:thetaT_hitting} $\theta_T(e)\ge\mathbb{P}_{\rho}\!\left(\tau_e<\tau_{\partial}\right)$.
\item\label{item:thetaT_sum} $\sum_{e:\:\ell(e)=1}\theta_T(e)\le \frac{1}{q_{\mathrm{esc}}}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
We present the proof of \eqref{item:thetaT_sum}.
The proofs of other items are simple using  \Cref{def:thetaT} and \Cref{nice:stopped_walk_transience}, and are omitted. Notice that for the edges in the first level, $\theta_T(e)$ only depends on the first $R$-ball. Consider a walk $Y$ from $\rho$ on the first $R$-ball and all long-range half-edges from it, which, every time it crosses a half-edge, gets terminated with probability $q_{\mathrm{esc}}$ and otherwise returns to the same vertex and continues. Then $\theta_T(e)=\mathbb{P}\!\left(Y\text{ hits }e\right)$. Therefore, if we set $L(Y)$ to be the number of different long-range half-edges $Y$ visits before it is terminated  \[\sum_{e:\:\ell(e)=1}\theta_T(e)= \sum_{e:\:\ell(e)=1}\mathbb{P}\!\left(Y \text{ hits }e\right)= \mathbb{E}\!\left[L(Y)\right]\le \frac{1}{q_{\mathrm{esc}}}\] as every time $Y$ visits a long-range half-edge it has probaility $q_{\mathrm{esc}}$ of being terminated.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{nice:bound_nontrunc_size}
There exists a positive constant $C$ such that for any realisation $T$ of a random quasi-tree, the number of balls in $T$ that can be reached from the root $\rho$ without crossing a truncated edge is $\le Ce^{C\log\log N}$, and all of these balls are at levels $\le C\log\log N$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Let us consider the finite tree $t_0$ obtained by removing the truncated edges of $T$, keeping only the connected component of $\rho$, and contracting each ball into a single vertex. By \Cref{nice:thetaT_properties}\eqref{item:thetaT_exp_decay} we know that $t_0$ has $\lesssim\log\log N$ levels.

Let $A_1$ denote the set of edges of $t_0$ leading to leaves. From \Cref{nice:thetaT_properties} \eqref{item:thetaT_multiplicative} and \eqref{item:thetaT_sum} and using that $t_0$ has $\lesssim\log\log N$ levels, we get that $\sum_{e\in A_1}\theta_{T}(e)\le q_{\mathrm{esc}}^{-C_1\log\log N}$ for some constant $C_1>0$. Then $|A_1|\le\frac{\log N}{c_{\mathrm{trunc}}}q_{\mathrm{esc}}^{-C_1\log\log N}\lesssim e^{C_2\log\log N}$ for some constant $C_2>0$.

Let $t_1$ be obtained by removing the edges in $A_1$ from $t_0$ (and the vertices that get disconnected from the root this way). Let $A_2$ be the set of edges leading to leaves in $t_1$. Similarly to the above, we see that $|A_2|\lesssim e^{C_2\log\log N}$. Continuing similarly, we see that the edges of $t_0$ can be partitioned into $\lesssim\log\log N$ `layers', each of which has $\lesssim e^{C_2\log\log N}$ edges. Hence $t_0$ has $\lesssim e^{C_2\log\log N}(\log\log N)\lesssim e^{C_3\log\log N}$ vertices where $C_3>0$ is a constant.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{prob_nice}
{For any given vertex $x$ in $G$ we have $\mathbb{P}\!\left(x\not\inV_{\mathrm{nice}}\right)\lesssim\frac{1}{(\log N)^{3/2}}$ and for any given $x$ and $y$ in $G$ we have $\mathbb{P}\!\left(x\text{ not nice in }G^*\setminus\{\{x,y\}\}\right)\lesssim\frac{1}{(\log N)^{3/2}}$.}  Furthermore, we have that whp $|V_{\mathrm{nice}}^c|\le \frac{N}{(\log N)^{4/3}}$.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let us explore the level $K$ neighbourhood of $x$ level by level.
From \Cref{volume_tail_bound} we know that with probability $1-o\left(\frac1N\right)$ the whole neighbourhood has volume $\lesssim e^{C(\log\log N)^2}$ where $C$ is a large constant. Every time the new endpoint of a red edge is revealed, the probability of it being any specific vertex is $\lesssim\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}$. Hence the probability of the neighbourhood having an overlap is $\lesssim\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}e^{2C(\log\log N)^2}\ll\frac{1}{(\log N)^2}$.

Now consider exploring (part of) the level $K$ neighbourhood of $x$ in $G_{\mathrm{rg}}$ by revealing balls as the walk $(X_t)_{t\le\tau_K}$ on $G_{\mathrm{rg}}$ started from $x$ first visits them. From \Cref{bound_atyp_prob} we know that for each newly revealed ball the probability that it is atypical is $\lesssim\left(\frac{1}{\log N}\right)^2$.

From \Cref{bound_sigma1} we know that for a sufficiently large $C$ the probability of $\tau_K\wedge\tau_{\partial}\wedge\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}\ge C(\log\log N)^{16}$ is $\lesssim\frac{1}{(\log N)^2}$. From \Cref{bound_atyp_prob} we know that the probability of any of the first $C(\log\log N)^{16}$ balls visited being atypical is $\lesssim\frac{(\log\log N)^{16}}{(\log N)^2}$. From the definition of typical balls, we know that the probability that the first $C(\log\log N)^{16}$ balls visited are all typical, but the walk hits the boundary in one of them, is $\lesssim\frac{(\log\log N)^{16}}{(\log N)^2}$.

Together these show that with probability $1-O\left(\frac{(\log\log N)^{16}}{(\log N)^2}\right)$ the walk visits $\le C(\log\log N)^{16}$ different vertices by $\tau_K$, and the events $\Omega_{\mathrm{typ}}\left(\tau_K\right)$ and $\Omega_{\partial}\left(\tau_K\right)$ hold.

Now let us reveal the blue degree of each vertex $X$ visits by time $\tau_K\wedge\tau_{\partial}\wedge\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}$ and let us consider a walk $\widehat{X}$ on $G^*$ that agrees with $X$ until $\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\wedge\tau_K\wedge\tau_{\partial}\wedge\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}$. For each of the first $C(\log\log N)^{16}$ different vertices visited by $X$, if we condition on the blue degrees of the previous vertices and work on the event that they sum to at most one, the probability of it having a blue edge is $\lesssim\frac{1}{\log N}$ and the probability of it having at least two blue edges is $\lesssim\frac{1}{(\log N)^2}$. Hence the probability of having more than one blue edge emanating from the first $C(\log\log N)^{16}$ different vertices visited by $X$ is $\lesssim\frac{(\log\log N)^{32}}{(\log N)^2}$.  Using Markov's inequality, this gives that with probability at least $ 1- \frac{1}{(\log N)^{3/2}}$ the graph $G^*$ and $x$ are such that with probability at least $1-\frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/3}}$ the walk starting from $x$ visits at most one vertex with exactly one blue edge and no vertices with more than one blue edges by  time $\tau_K$. 
By \Cref{transience_until_nonbinary} for any realisation of the graph, the probability that $X$ revisits a given vertex $v$ more than $C'\deg(v)$ times by $\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\wedge\tau_K\wedge\tau_{\partial}\wedge\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}$ is $\le\varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon$ can be made arbitrarily small by choosing $C'$ sufficiently large. Applying this to the first vertex visited by $X$ that has a blue half-edge, we see that with positive probability $\widehat{X}$ does not cross the blue half-edge from this vertex by time $\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}\wedge\tau_K\wedge\tau_{\partial}\wedge\tau_{\mathrm{atyp}}$.

Combining the above estimates finishes the proof of the first part.

The proof of the second part is analogous to the first one. The third part follows from the first one and Markov's inequality, as the expected number of vertices which are not nice is at most $\frac{N}{(\log N)^{3/2}}$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
From \Cref{volume_tail_bound}, we know that each time a new ball is revealed in $T$, with probability $1-o\left(\frac{1}{N^2}\right)$, its volume plus the total number of half-edges emanating from it is $\le e^{C_1R}$ where $C_1$ is a positive constant. For any $c_2>0$ we can get $e^{C_1R}\le e^{c_2\log N}$ by choosing $c_R$ sufficiently small. By \Cref{nice:bound_nontrunc_size} the number of balls in the explored region of $T$ is $\lesssim e^{C_3\log\log N}$ for some $C_3>0$, so the overall volume of this region plus the number of half-edges from it is $\lesssim e^{c_2\log N}e^{C_3\log\log N}$, which can be made $\le e^{c_4\log N}$ for any $c_4>0$.

We will show that each time a new ball in $T$ is revealed, on the event that the total number of already revealed vertices plus half-edges is $\lesssim N^{c_4}$, the probability that the new ball has an overlap or its optimal coupling with the ball in $G^*$ fails is
\begin{align}\label{eq:nice:bound_overlap_prob}
\lesssim N^{c_4+c_2}\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}+\mathbb{P}\!\left(|B_{R+1}|\ge N^{c_2}\right).
\end{align}

Using this we see that the probability that there is more than one instance when there is an overlap or the optimal coupling fails is $\le\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathrm{Bin}\!\left(C_5N^{c_4},C_6\frac{N^{c_4+c_2}}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}\right)>1\right)+C_5N^{c_4}\mathbb{P}\!\left(|B_{R+1}|\ge N^{c_2}\right)$, which is $o\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)$ for sufficiently small values of $c_2$ and $c_4$, and sufficiently small values of $c_R$ in terms of $c_2$.

We can prove \eqref{eq:nice:bound_overlap_prob} as follows.  For a set of vertices $S$ let $\Gamma(S)$ denote the set of points that are in $S$ or adjacent to a vertex in $S$ in $G^*$.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the set of already explored vertices and let $e$ be a given half-edge from $\mathcal{A}$. Let $Z=e^{+}$ be the other endpoint of $e$, let $\mathcal{B}(Z)$ be the $R$-ball in green and black edges around $Z$ and let $\mathcal{B}$ be an independent copy of an  $R$-ball in green and black edges in $G^*$ centred at the origin. Then for any values of $A$, $\Gamma_{A}$, $e'_{-}$, $z$, $B$ and $\Gamma_B$ with $(z+\Gamma_B)\cap\Gamma_A=\emptyset$ and $(e_{-}',z)\notin z+\Gamma_B$ we have
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}\left(Z=z,\mathcal{B}(Z)=z+B,\Gamma(\mathcal{B}(Z))={(z+\Gamma_B)\cup (e_{-}',z)}\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{A}=A,\Gamma(\mathcal{A})=\Gamma_A,e_{-}=e'_{-}\right)\qquad\qquad&\\
\quad=\quad\mathbb{P}\left(Z=z,\mathcal{B}=B',\Gamma(\mathcal{B})=\Gamma_B\;\middle\vert\;e_{-}=e'_{-}\right).&
\end{align*}

This shows that the probability that the optimal coupling succeeds and that there is no overlap can be lower bounded by the probability that $Z$, $\mathcal{B}$ and $\Gamma(\mathcal{B})$ satisfy $(Z+\Gamma(\mathcal{B}))\cap\Gamma_A=\emptyset$ and $(e_{-}',Z)\notin Z+\Gamma_B$ for a given realisation of $A',\Gamma'_A, e'_{-}$.

For any realisation of $\Gamma_B$ and $\Gamma_A$ we have $\#\left\{z:\:(z+\Gamma_B)\cap\Gamma_A\ne\emptyset\right\}\le|\Gamma_A|\cdot|\Gamma_B|$, for any specific value of $z$ we have $\mathbb{P}\!\left(Z=z\right)\lesssim\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}$ and the probability that any specific red or blue edge $(e_{-}'-z,0)$ is in $
\Gamma(\mathcal{B})$ is at most $\lesssim\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}$. Therefore, the probability of overlap or coupling failing given the realisation of $e_{-}, \Gamma(\mathcal{A}), \Gamma(\mathcal{B})$ is bounded by
\begin{align*}& \mathbb{P}\left(Z\in \left\{z:\:(z+\Gamma_B)\cap\Gamma_A\ne\emptyset\right\}\;\middle\vert\;\Gamma(\mathcal{A})=\Gamma_A,e_{-}=e'_{-}, \Gamma(\mathcal{B})=\Gamma_B\right)
\\&+ \mathbb{P}\left((e'_{-},Z)\in Z+\Gamma_B\;\middle\vert\;\Gamma(\mathcal{A})=\Gamma_A,e_{-}=e'_{-}, \Gamma(\mathcal{B})=\Gamma_B\right)\lesssim \frac{|\Gamma_A||\Gamma_B|+1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}
\end{align*}
and using the assumption $|\Gamma(\mathcal{A})|\le N^{c_4}$ the desired inequality follows.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
\label{def:cool_box}
Let $r$ be a large constant to be chosen later. Let us partition the torus $G$ into boxes of side length $r$. Let us call a box \emph{cool} if in $G^*$ there are at least two red edges emanating from it, and each of its vertices has degree $\led_{\mathrm{cool}}$, where $d_{\mathrm{cool}}$ is a constant to be chosen later.
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The following arguments would also work if we considered blue and red edges instead of just red ones.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{nice:visit_many_cool_boxes}
Let $C_{\mathrm{cool}}$ be any constant. Then for sufficiently large values of $r$ and $d_{\mathrm{cool}}$ the following holds. For any vertex $x$ of $G$, with probability $1-o\left(\frac1N\right)$, the graph $G^*$ is such that {with high probability} a walk $X$ on it from $x$ visits $\ge\frac{R}{dr}$ different boxes before reaching graph distance $R$ from $x$, and out of the first $\frac{R}{dr}$ different boxes visited $\geC_{\mathrm{cool}}\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}=:t_{\mathrm{cool}}$ are cool.
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{nice:cross_many_red_edges}
Fix any vertex $x$ of $G$, and consider any realisation of $G^*$ with at least $\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}$ cool boxes. Then with high probability a walk $X$ on $G^*$ from $x$ crosses $\ge\frac{\log N}{(\log\log N)^2}$ different red edges by the time it visits $\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}$ different cool boxes.
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{nice:reach_level_CloglogN}
For any positive constant $C$, the following holds. For any realisation of the quasi-tree $T$, with high probability a walk $X$ on it from its root $x$ reaches level $C\log\log N$ of $T$ or hits the boundary of a ball before crossing $\frac{\log N}{(\log\log N)^2}$ different red edges.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Let us explore parts of $G^*$ as the walk visits them. First, let us reveal the green, red and blue degrees of each vertex in the box containing $x$. This will in particular tell us whether the box is cool. Then always proceed with the exploration as follows. Take steps with the walk. If the walk steps along a green, red or blue half-edge whose other endpoint is not revealed yet, then sample the other endpoint of the half-edge with the correct distribution and let the walk step there. If the walk enters a box that has not been visited before, then reveal the green, red and blue degrees of the box, hence also revealing whether the box is cool.

Each box has diameter $\le dr$, hence the walk visits at least $\frac{R}{dr}$ different boxes before reaching graph distance $R$ from $x$.

 We will now show that there is a small constant $c$ and a large constant $C$ such that the first $\frac{R}{dr}$ times that a box is visited for the first time, that box has probability at least $1-p_{\mathrm{uncool}}$ of being cool, regardless of what was explored so far, where $p_{\mathrm{uncool}}\le C\left( e^{-cr^d}+\frac{r^d}{d_{\mathrm{cool}}}\right)$. Indeed, assume that the above process has so far revealed $<\frac{R}{dr}$ different boxes and that the walk now steps into a new box and let the box have vertices labelled by $v_1$, ..., $v_{r^d}$. As $\frac{R}{dr}r^d= N^{o(1)}$ for each of these $v_i$s the probability of having a red edge leading to one of the yet unrevealed vertices is lower bounded by a positive constant, meaning that the probability that the box has fewer than $2$ red edges can be upper bounded by $e^{-\text{const}(r^d-1)}(r^d+1)\le Ce^{-cr^d}$. To bound the probability of any of the vertices having degree larger than $d_{\mathrm{cool}}$, first notice that the expected sum of green, red and blue degrees to yet unrevealed vertices is upper bounded by the expected sum of green, red and blue degrees of a vertex in a graph where nothing was revealed, which is $1$. We know by \Cref{max_deg} that the probability of any vertex having degree $>d_{\mathrm{max}}$ is $o\left(\frac1N\right)$. Even if all of the so far revealed vertices had degree $d_{\mathrm{max}}$, using \Cref{cond_green_red_deg}  we get that the expected number of edges between these and a given $v_i$ is $\lesssimd_{\mathrm{max}}\sum_{y:\:|y|\le\left(\frac{R}{dr}r^d\right)^{\frac1d}}p_{0,y}\lesssim\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\sum_{y:\:|y|\le(C\log N)^{\frac1d}}\frac{1}{\log N}\frac{1}{|y|^d}\asymp1$. Markov's inequality gives that the probability of at least one $v_i$ having degree $>d_{\mathrm{cool}}$ is $\lesssim\frac{r^d}{d_{\mathrm{cool}}}$. 



Using these and \Cref{Bin_rough_tail_bound} we get that the probability of seeing less than $t_{\mathrm{cool}}$ different cool boxes is
\begin{align*}
&\le\:\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathrm{Bin}\!\left(\frac{R}{dr},1-p_{\mathrm{uncool}}\right)\let_{\mathrm{cool}}\right)\:\le\:\left(\frac{R}{dr}\right)^{t_{\mathrm{cool}}}p_{\mathrm{uncool}}^{\frac{R}{dr}-t_{\mathrm{cool}}}\:\le\:\left(\frac{R}{dr}\right)^{t_{\mathrm{cool}}}\left(Ce^{-cr^d}+C\frac{r^d}{d_{\mathrm{cool}}}\right)^{\frac12\frac{R}{dr}}
\\&=\:\exp\left(C_{\mathrm{cool}}\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\left(\log\log N-\log\left(\frac{dr}{c_R}\right)\right)+\frac12\frac{c_R \log N}{dr}\log\left(Ce^{-cr^d}+C\frac{r^d}{d_{\mathrm{cool}}}\right)\right)
\end{align*}
This can be made $\ll\frac{1}{N^2}$ by setting $r$ sufficiently large in terms of $C_{\mathrm{cool}}, C, c, c_R$ and $d$, so that $C_{\mathrm{cool}}+\log(2C)\frac{c_R}{2dr}-r^{d-1}c\frac{c_R}{2d}<-2 $ and setting $d_{\mathrm{cool}}$ to satisfy $r^de^{cr^d}\le d_{\mathrm{cool}}$. The proof now follows by Markov's inequality.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Note that each time the walk $X$ enters a cool box, there is a positive probability that it exits the box via a red edge that is different from the edge it entered through. Say this probability is at least $q$ where $q$ is a small positive constant depending on $r$ and $d_{\mathrm{cool}}$.

Then the probability of the walk crossing $<\frac{\log N}{(\log\log N)^2}$ different red edges by the time it visits $\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}$ different cool boxes is
\[
\le\quad\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathrm{Bin}\!\left(\frac{\log N}{\log\log N},q\right)<\frac{\log N}{(\log\log N)^2}\right)\quad\ll\quad1.\qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Let $\ell\in\left\{1,...,C\log\log N\right\}$. We know from \Cref{nice:stopped_walk_transience} that every time the walk crosses from level $(\ell-1)$ to level $\ell$, there is a positive probability that it will not return to level $(\ell-1)$ without hitting the boundary of a ball first. Therefore the probability of crossing from level $(\ell-1)$ to $\ell$ more than $\frac{\log N}{C(\log\log N)^3}$ times without hitting a boundary is $\ll\frac{1}{\log\log N}$. Taking the union bound over $\ell$ gives the result.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{bound_sum_of_first_k_deg}
For any $C_0>0$ there exists a $C>0$ such that for any $c\in(0,C_0)$ the following is satisfied. For any $x$, with probability $1-o\left(\frac1N\right)$, the graph $G^*$ is such that, whp, the sum of the degrees of the first $c\log N$ different vertices visited by a walk $X$ from $x$ is $\le Cc\log N$.
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Let us explore (part of) the graph $G^*$ as we take steps with the walk $X$ as follows.

If the walk $X$ is at a vertex $v$ that is visited for the first time, let us sample the green, red and blue degrees of $v$ according to the correct distributions based on what we have revealed so far. Then pick one of the half-edges from $X$ uniformly randomly and if its other endpoint is not known yet, let us sample it according to the correct distribution. Then let $X$ step to the other endpoint of the edge.

If the walk $X$ is at a vertex $v$ that has been visited before, then we already know the green, red and blue degree of $v$. Let us pick a half-edge from $v$ uniformly at random, if its other endpoint is not revealed yet, then sample it according to the correct distribution, and let $X$ step to the other endpoint of the edge.

Let us continue this until $X$ visits $c\log N$ different vertices. Let $v_k$ denote the $k$th new vertex visited (let $v_0=x$) and let $\mathcal{H}_{k-1}$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by everything we know until then. Using \Cref{cond_green_red_deg} and the independence of edges of different colours, we get that for any realisation of $\mathcal{H}_{k-1}$ with $\deg(v_i)\ll\log N$ for all $i\in\{0,1,...,k-1\}$ we have
\begin{align*}
\left(d_{\mathrm{g}}(v_k),d_{\mathrm{r}}(v_k),d_{\mathrm{b}}(v_k)\mid\mathcal{H}_{k-1}\right)\quad\le_{\mathrm{st}}\quad\left(\sum_{y}B_{g,y},\:\sum_{y}B_{r,y},\:\sum_{y}B_{b,y}\right)
\end{align*}
where $B_{g,y}$, $B_{r,y}$ and $B_{b,y}$ are independent Bernoulli random variables, with $B_{g,y}$, $B_{r,y}$ and $B_{b,y}$ having parameters $p^{\mathrm{green}}_{v_k,y}$, $p^{\mathrm{red}}_{v_k,y}$ and $p^{\mathrm{blue}}_{v_k,y}$ respectively for $y\not\in\{v_0,...,v_{k-1}\}$, and having parameters $C_1d_{\mathrm{g}}(y)p^{\mathrm{green}}_{v_k,y}$, $C_1d_{\mathrm{r}}(y)p^{\mathrm{red}}_{v_k,y}$ and $C_1(\log N)d_{\mathrm{b}}(y)p^{\mathrm{blue}}_{v_k,y}$ respectively for $y\in\{v_0,...,v_{k-1}\}$, where $C_1$ is a positive constant.

If $k\le C_0\log N$ and $d_{\mathrm{g}}(v_i),d_{\mathrm{r}}(v_i),d_{\mathrm{b}}(v_i)\le C_2\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}$ for all $i\in\{0,1,...,k-1\}$, then we have 
\begin{align*}
\left(\sum_{y}B_{g,y},\:\sum_{y}B_{r,y},\:\sum_{y}B_{b,y}\right)\quad\le_{\mathrm{st}}\quad\left(\sum_{y}I_{g,y},\:\sum_{y}I_{r,y},\:\sum_{y}I_{b,y}\right)
\end{align*}
where $I_{g,y}$, $I_{r,y}$ and $I_{b,y}$ are independent Bernoulli random variables, with $I_{g,y}$ and $I_{b,y}$ having parameters $C_1C_2\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}p^{\mathrm{green}}_{0,y}$ and $C_1C_2\frac{(\log N)^2}{\log\log N}p^{\mathrm{blue}}_{0,y}$ respectively for the $C_0\log N$ vertices $y$ with the smallest graph distance from $0$; $I_{g,y}$ and $I_{b,y}$ having parameters $p^{\mathrm{green}}_{0,y}$ and $p^{\mathrm{blue}}_{0,y}$ respectively for the other vertices $y$; $I_{r,y}$ having parameter $C_1C_2\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}p^{\mathrm{red}}_{0,y}$ for the $C_0\log N$ vertices $y$ that have the smallest graph distance from $0$ while satisfying $|y|>D^{1-\beta}$; and $I_{r,y}$ having parameter $p^{\mathrm{red}}_{0,y}$ for the other vertices $y$\footnote{{The stochastic domination follows from the fact that if $p>q$ and $s>1$ then for independent Bernoulli random variables we have $\mathrm{Bern}\!\left(p\right)+\mathrm{Bern}\!\left(sq\right)\le_{\mathrm{st}}\mathrm{Bern}\!\left(sp\right)+\mathrm{Bern}\!\left(q\right)$.}}.

Let $(I_{g,k,y},I_{r,k,y},I_{b,k,y})$ be independent copies of $(I_{g,y},I_{r,y},I_{b,y})$ for each $k$. Then by the above, there exists a coupling between $(G^*,X)$ and $(I_{g,k,y},I_{r,k,y},I_{b,k,y})_{k}$ such that on the event that $\deg(v_k)\le C_2\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}$ for all $k\le C_0\log N$, we have $d_{\mathrm{g}}(v_k)\le\sum_{y}I_{g,k,y}$, $d_{\mathrm{r}}(v_k)\le\sum_{y}I_{r,k,y}$ and $d_{\mathrm{b}}(v_k)\le\sum_{y}I_{b,k,y}$ for all $k\le C_0\log N$.

Note that $\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{y}I_{g,y}\right]\asymp\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{y}I_{r,y}\right]\asymp1$ and $\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{y}I_{b,y}\right]\ll1$, hence from \Cref{sum_of_Berns} we get that for sufficiently large $C$ for any $c\le C_0$ we have
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}\!\left(\sum_{k=0}^{c\log N}\sum_{y}(I_{g,k,y}+I_{r,k,y}+I_{b,k,y})\ge Cc\log N\right)\quad \le\quad\exp\left(-C_3\log N\right),
\end{align*}
where $C_3$ is a constant that can be made arbitrarily large by choosing $C$ large. In particular, we get a $o\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)$ bound if $C$ is sufficiently large.

From \Cref{max_deg} we know that with probability $1-o\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)$ the graph $G^*$ is such that all vertices have degree $\le C_2\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}$ where $C_2$ is a sufficiently large constant.

Putting these estimates together and using Markov's inequality finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{edge_expected_num_crossings}
For any realisation $T$ of a random quasi-tree and any directed edge $(x,y)$ in $T$, the expected number of times a walk on $T$ started from $x$ or $y$ crosses $(x,y)$ before hitting the boundary can be bounded as
\[
\mathbb{E}_{y}\!\left[\#\text{crossings of }(x,y)\text{ by time }\tau_{\partial}\right]\quad\le\quad\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\#\text{crossings of }(x,y)\text{ by time }\tau_{\partial}\right]\quad\lesssim\quad1.
\]
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
The $\le$ is immediate. The $\lesssim$ can be derived as follows.
\begin{align*}
&\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\#\text{crossings of }(x,y)\text{ by }\tau_{\partial}\right]\quad=\quad\sum_{k\ge0}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(\ge k\text{ returns to }x\text{ by }\tau_{\partial},\text{ step to }y\text{ after the }k\text{th one}\right)\\
&=\quad\sum_{k\ge0}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(\ge k\text{ returns to }x\text{ by }\tau_{\partial}\right)\frac{1}{\deg(x)}\quad\lesssim\quad1,
\end{align*}
where in the last estimate we used \Cref{nice:stopped_walk_transience}.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{nice:reach_range_clogN}
For any $C_0>0$ and $\theta\in(0,1)$ there exists a $C>0$ such that for any $c\in(0,C_0)$ the following is satisfied. For any $x$, with probability $1-o\left(\frac1N\right)$, the graph $G^*$ is such that with probability at least $1-\theta$ the time it takes for a walk $X$ from $x$ on the quasi-tree $T(G^*)$ induced by $G^*$ to visit $c\log N$ different vertices or hit the boundary of a ball is $\le Cc\log N$.
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Let $s:=c\log N$ and let $\alpha_s$ be the number of steps it takes for the walk to visit $s$ different vertices.
By \Cref{bound_sum_of_first_k_deg} we know that w.p.\ $1-o\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)$ the graph $G^*$ is such that whp the degrees of the first $s$ different vertices visited by $X$ sum to $\le C_1s$ where $C_1$ is a large positive constant. If the degrees sum to $\le C_1s$ then by time $\alpha_s$ the walk crosses at most $C_1s$ different directed edges. Let $e_k$ be the $k$th new directed edge crossed. By \Cref{edge_expected_num_crossings} the expected number of total crossings of $e_1$, ..., $e_{C_1s}$ by time $\tau_{\partial}$ is $\le C_2C_1s$ where $C_2$ is a large constant. Markov's inequality gives that with prob $\ge1-\frac12\theta$ the number of crossings is $\le \frac2\theta C_2C_1s$, hence $\alpha_s\le\frac2\theta C_2C_1s$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Note that on the event that the exploration of \Cref{def:nbhd_for_hitting_nice} succeeds, a walk on $T$ can be coupled to a walk on $T(G^*)$ so that they agree until they first hit $A\cup\{\widetilde{e}\}$.


From \Cref{nice:bound_nontrunc_size} we know that the walk on $T(G^*)$ hits $A\cup\{\widetilde{e}\}$ by the time it reaches level $C\log\log N$, where $C$ is a large constant. Combining \Cref{nice:visit_many_cool_boxes}, \Cref{nice:cross_many_red_edges} and \Cref{nice:reach_level_CloglogN} we get that with probability $1-o\left(\frac1N\right)$ the graph $G^*$ is such that with high probability the walk $X$ on $T(G^*)$ reaches level $C\log\log N$ or hits $\partial$ by the time it reaches graph distance $R$ from $x$. {This shows \eqref{item:nice:not_hit_boundary}.} Also, whp the walk visits $\le\frac{r^{d-1}c_R}{d}\log N$ different vertices by the time it reaches level $C\log\log N$ or hits $\partial$. This proves \eqref{item:nice:bound_num_visited}.

From \Cref{nice:reach_range_clogN} we also get \eqref{item:nice:bound_time}. Part \eqref{item:nice:not_hit_etil} follows from \Cref{nice:stopped_walk_transience}, and part \eqref{item:nice:bound_prob_given_e} follows by noting that by definition $\theta_T(e)\le\frac{c_{\mathrm{trunc}}}{\log N}$ for all $e\in A$, and by \Cref{nice:thetaT_properties} we have $\mathbb{P}_{\rho}\!\left(\tau_e<\tau_{\partial}\right)\le\theta_T(e)$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
There exist positive constants $c_1$ and $c_2$, not depending on the choice of $c_{\mathrm{trunc}}$, and a positive constant $C_3$, with the following property. For any $k\in\{1,2,...,a\}$ and any realisation of the exploration in the first $(k-1)$ steps such that $\Omega_{\mathrm{nbhd}}$ is satisfied, and the number of explored vertices and long-range edges is $\le N^{c_1}$, we have
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(I_k=1\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_{k-1}\right)\quad&\ge\quad c_2,\\
\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\#\left(\text{vertices and half-edges revealed in step }k\right)\le e^{C_3(\log\log N)^2}\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_{k-1}\right) \quad&=\quad1-o\left(\frac{1}{N^2}\right).
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
The second bound follows from \Cref{volume_tail_bound}. We can prove the first bound as follows.

Let $y=e_k^-$ be the endpoint of $e_k$ in the already explored region. For a given vertex $z$ we know from \Cref{prob_nice} that without any conditioning we would have $\mathbb{P}\!\left(z\text{ not nice in }G^*\setminus\{\{y,z\}\}\right)\lesssim\frac{1}{(\log N)^{3/2}}$. Also, for any given $z$ we have $\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(e_k^+=z\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_{k-1}\right)\lesssim\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}$. Similarly to the proof of \Cref{nice:coupling_success_and_nbhd_size} we  can couple a copy of the unconditioned graph $G^*\setminus\{\{y,z\}\}$ and a copy of $\left(G^*\setminus\{\{y,z\}\}\mid\mathcal{G}_{k-1},\:e_k^+=z\right)$ such that on the event that the level $K$ neighbourhood of $z$ in $G^*\setminus\{\{y,z\}\}$ does not intersect the set of explored vertices in $\left(G^*\setminus\{\{y,z\}\}\mid\mathcal{G}_{k-1},\:e_k^+=z\right)$, the level $K$ neighbourhood of $z$ agrees in the two copies.

Because of this, we can write
\begin{align*}
&\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(z\text{ is not almost nice with distinguished edge }\{y,z\}\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_{k-1},\:e_k^+=z\right)\quad\\
&\le\mathbb{P}\!\left(z\text{ not nice in }G^*\setminus\{\{y,z\}\}\right)\\
&\:+\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\text{the level }K\text{ nbhd of }z\text{ in an indep copy of }G^*\setminus\{\{y,z\}\}\text{ intersects the explored region}\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_{k-1}\right).
\end{align*}

Then for sufficiently small values of $c_1$ (for $c_1<1-\beta$) we have
\begin{align*}
&\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(e_k\text{ not nice}\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_{k-1}\right)\quad\\
&=\quad\sum_{z}\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(e_k^+=z\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_{k-1}\right)\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(z\text{ is not almost nice with distinguished edge }\{y,z\}\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_{k-1},\:e_k^+=z\right)\\
&\lesssim\quad\sum_{z}\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(e_k^+=z\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_{k-1}\right)\frac{1}{(\log N)^{3/2}}\\
&\quad+\quad\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\#(z\text{ within graph dist. }C_KC_R(\log\log N)^2\text{ from the explored region})\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_{k-1}\right]\\
&\lesssim\quad\frac{1}{(\log N)^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}N^{c_1}e^{C_3(\log\log N)^2}+\frac{1}{N^{1-\beta}\log N}N\frac{1}{N^2}\quad\lesssim\quad\frac{1}{(\log N)^{3/2}}\quad\ll\quad1,
\end{align*}
where in the first inequality we have used that the set of vertices $z$ whose level-$K$ neighbourhood intersects the explored region is a subset of the set of vertices which have graph distance at most $C_KC_R(\log\log N)^2$ from the explored region. In the second inequality, we use that the probability that all $C_KC_R(\log\log N)^2$ balls in $G^*$ have size at most $e^{C_3(\log\log N)^2}$ is at least $1-\frac{1}{N^2}$, and we otherwise bound the quantity in the expectation by $N$.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
We have just shown that there exists a constant $c_2$, not depending on any of the parameters, such that for any realisation of $\mathcal{G}_0$ satisfying $\Omega_{\mathrm{nbhd}}$, we can couple $(I_k)$ with a sequence $(J_k)$ of iid $\mathrm{Bern}\!\left(c_2\right)$ random variables such that with probability $1-o\left(\frac1N\right)$ we have $I_k\ge J_k$ for all $k$. Using this, using that on $\Omega_{\mathrm{nbhd}}$ we have $\sum_{k}q_k\ge c_4$ (where $c_4$ is a positive constant, not depending on any other parameters) and $q_k\le\frac{c_{\mathrm{trunc}}}{\log N}$ for all $k$, and using the concentration bound in \Cref{sum_indep_RVs} we get that on $\Omega_{\mathrm{nbhd}}$ we have
\begin{align*}
&\mathbb{P}_{}\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{a}q_kI_k\le\frac12c_2c_4\;\middle\vert\;\mathcal{G}_0\right)\quad\le\quad\mathbb{P}\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{a}q_kJ_k\le\frac12c_2c_4\right)+o\left(\frac1N\right)\quad\\
&=\quad\mathbb{P}\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{a}\frac{\log N}{c_{\mathrm{trunc}}}q_kJ_k\le\frac{c_2c_4}{2c_{\mathrm{trunc}}}\log N\right)+o\left(\frac1N\right)\quad \le\quad\exp\left(-\frac{3c_2c_4}{20c_{\mathrm{trunc}}}\log N\right)+o\left(\frac1N\right).
\end{align*}
By choosing $c_{\mathrm{trunc}}$ sufficiently small, we can make the right-hand side $o\left(\frac1N\right)$.

Using this and \Cref{nice:nbhd_properties} with a sufficiently small $\theta'$ in \eqref{item:nice:bound_time}, we get that there is a constant $C$ depending on $\theta'$ such that for any starting vertex $x$, with probability $1-o\left(\frac1N\right)$ the graph $G^*$ is such that with probability at least $\theta'$ a walk from $x$ hits an almost nice vertex in $\le C\log N$ steps. By the union bound, we now know that whp the graph is such that for all starting points, with probability at least $\theta'$, the walk hits an almost nice vertex in $C\log N$ steps. Then, using repeated trials, we also see that for any $\theta\in(0,1)$ with probability at least $\theta$ the walk hits an almost nice vertex in $\lesssim\log N$ steps, uniformly over the starting point. This finishes the proof of \Cref{hit_almost_nice_quickly}.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-37: body_md -->
\label{most_blue_nice}
Let $p^{\mathrm{blue}}=\frac{c_{\mathrm{b}}}{N\log N}$ where $c_{\mathrm{b}}\asymp1$. Then for any $\theta\in(0,1)$ there exists $C>0$ such that whp the following properties hold. The set $\mathcal{A}:=\left\{y\inV_{\mathrm{nice}}:\:d_{\mathrm{b}}(y)\ge1\right\}$ has size $|\mathcal{A}|\le (1+\theta)c_{\mathrm{b}}\frac{N}{\log N}$. The set $\mathcal{A}_C:=\left\{y\in\mathcal{A}:\:\deg(y)\le C,d_{\mathrm{b}}(y)= 1, \text{ and } \deg(z)\le C\, \mathrm{for}\, z\text{ with }z\sim_{\mathrm{b}} y\right\}$ has size $|\mathcal{A}_C|\ge(1-\theta)c_{\mathrm{b}}\frac{N}{\log N}$. For any $x\inV'_{\mathrm{nice}}$ the set $\mathcal{A}_x:=\left\{y\in\mathcal{A}:\:K\text{-neighbourhoods of }x,y\text{ are disjoint}\right\}$ has size $|\mathcal{A}_x|\ge(1-\theta)c_{\mathrm{b}}\frac{N}{\log N}$.
<!-- end lemma-37 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Throughout the proof, the probabilities are conditional on $G^*$, but this is dropped from the notation. {We work on the high probability event that $G^*$ satisfies the statement of \Cref{hit_almost_nice_quickly} with $\theta=\frac78$, the statement of \Cref{transition_probs_on_Vnice} and the statement of \Cref{most_blue_nice} with a sufficiently small value of $\theta$.}

\begin{itemize}
\item Let $C_1$ be the constant from \Cref{hit_almost_nice_quickly} such that for any starting point with probability at least $\frac78$ we have $\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}\le C_1\log N$, where $\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}$ denotes the first time that the walk visits $V'_{\mathrm{nice}}$. Let $C_2$ be the constant bounding $\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}^{(2)}}{\log N}$ in \Cref{transition_probs_on_Vnice}.
\item Let us consider any $x\in V$. If $x\inV'_{\mathrm{nice}}$ then let $\mathcal{A}_x$ be as in \Cref{most_blue_nice}, while if $x\not\inV'_{\mathrm{nice}}$, let $\mathcal{A}_x:=\left\{z:\:\sum_{y\in V'_{\mathrm{nice}}}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}}=y,\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}\le C_1\log N\right)\1{z\in\mathcal{A}_y}\ge\frac12\right\}$. (Note that this latter definition is also consistent for $x\inV'_{\mathrm{nice}}$.) Intuitively, $\mathcal{A}_x$ is the set of nice vertices with blue edges for which there is probability at least $\frac12$ that their $K$-neighbourhoods are disjoint from the $K$-neighbourhood of the first nice vertex that a walk from $x$ hits. (If the walk does not hit a nice vertex by time $C_1\log N$, then the second neighbourhood is treated as not well-defined and the neighbourhoods are not treated as disjoint).
\item {We can lower bound the size of $|\mathcal{A}_x|$ as follows.
\begin{align*}
|\mathcal{A}_x|\quad&=\quad\sum_{z\in\mathcal{A}}\1{\sum_{y}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}}=y,\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}\le C_1\log N\right)\1{z\in\mathcal{A}_y}\ge\frac12}\quad\\
&\ge \quad\sum_{z\in\mathcal{A}}\left(2\sum_{y}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}}=y,\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}\le C_1\log N\right)\1{z\in\mathcal{A}_y}-1\right)\\
&=\quad2\sum_{y}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}}=y,\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}\le C_1\log N\right)|\mathcal{A}_y|\quad-\quad|\mathcal{A}|
\end{align*}
By \Cref{most_blue_nice} we have $|\mathcal{A}_y|\ge(1-\theta)c_b\frac{N}{\log N}$ for all $y$ and $|\mathcal{A}|\le(1+\theta)c_b\frac{N}{\log N}$. Using this and that $\sum_{y}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}}=y,\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}\le C_1\log N\right)\ge\frac78$ we get that $|\mathcal{A}_x|\ge\left(\frac34-\frac{11}{4}\theta\right)c_b\frac{N}{\log N}$.}
\item Let $\tau_1=\tau_{\mathrm{nice}'}\wedge C_1\log N$ and let $\tau_2=\tau_{\mathrm{blue}}^{(2)}\wedge C_2\log N$.
\item For any $x\in V$ and $z\in\mathcal{A}_x$, using \Cref{transition_probs_on_Vnice} and the definition of $\mathcal{A}_x$ we get that
\begin{align}\label{eq:Xtau1tau2}
&\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_1+\tau_2-1}=z\right)\quad=\quad\sum_{y}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_1}=y\right)\mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_{\tau_2-1}=z\right)\quad\\
\nonumber
&\ge\quad\sum_{y}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_1}=y\right)\1{z\in\mathcal{A}_y}\mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_{\tau_2-1}=z\right)\quad
\gtrsim\quad\sum_{y}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_1}=y\right)\1{z\in\mathcal{A}_y}\frac{\log N}{N}\:\gtrsim\:\frac{\log N}{N}.
\end{align}
\item Let $C_3=C_1+C_2$ and let $\tau_3\sim\mathrm{Unif}\!\left(\{1,...,C_3\log N+1\}\right)$, independently of everything else. Let $C$ be a sufficiently large constant, to be specified later.
\item We will now show that for any $x,y\in V$ we have,
\begin{align*}
&\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_1+\tau_2+\tau_3}=y\right)\quad\ge\quad\sum_{{z\in\mathcal{A}_x\cap\mathcal{A}_y\cap\mathcal{A}_C}}\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_1+\tau_2-1}=z, X_{\tau_1+\tau_2+1}=z\right)\mathbb{P}_{z}\!\left(X_{\tau_3-1}=y\right)\\
&\gtrsim\quad\frac{\log N}{N}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{A}_x\cap\mathcal{A}_y\cap\mathcal{A}_C}\frac{1}{\log N}\sum_{k=0}^{C_3\log N}\mathbb{P}_{z}\!\left(X_k=y\right)\:
=\:\frac{1}{N}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{A}_x\cap\mathcal{A}_y\cap\mathcal{A}_C}\sum_{k=0}^{C_3\log N}\frac{\deg(y)}{\deg(z)}\mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_k=z\right)\\
&\gtrsim\quad\frac{\deg(y)}{N}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{A}_x\cap\mathcal{A}_y\cap\mathcal{A}_C}\mathbb{P}_{y}\!\left(X_{\tau_1+\tau_2-1}=z\right)\quad\gtrsim\quad\frac{\deg(y)}{N}\left|\mathcal{A}_x\cap\mathcal{A}_y\cap\mathcal{A}_C\right|\frac{\log N}{N}.
\end{align*}
For the second inequality, we used~\eqref{eq:Xtau1tau2} and the fact that each $z\in\mathcal{A}_C$ has blue degree 1 and its blue neighbour has degree at most $C$, so the probability that the walk immediately backtracks the blue edge crossed at $z$ is at least $\frac{1}{C}\gtrsim 1$. For the penultimate inequality, we used that by definition $\tau_1+\tau_2\le C_3\log N$, while for the final inequality we used~\eqref{eq:Xtau1tau2} again. Intuitively, the above inequalities say the following. The probability of getting from any $x$ to any $y$ in time $\tau_1+\tau_2+\tau_3$  can be lower bounded by summing over all suitable $z$ \footnote{More precisely, the sum is over all nice $z$ with one blue edge which likely have disjoint $K$-neighbourhood from the first nice vertex walk from $x$ or from $y$ would hit and which have bounded degree and for which the other endpoint of their blue edge has bounded degree. The number of such vertices is of the same order as the number of vertices with blue edges.} the probability that the walk from $x$ crosses a blue edge at $z$ at time $\tau_1+\tau_2$, goes back on that edge immediately (this is why we require the other endpoint to have bounded degree) and then hits $y$ in another $\tau_3-1$ steps. The probability of hitting $y$ from $z$ after reversing is a suitable ratio of degrees times the probability that at time $\tau_3-1$ the walk from $y$ hits $z$. However, as  $z$ has one blue edge and bounded degree, there is a constant probability that if the walk is at $z$ at time $\tau_3-1$, it would go on to cross that blue edge in the next time step. Moreover, as $\tau_1+\tau_2\le C_3\log N$, by definition, this means that we can lower bound the probability of getting from $y$ to $z$ at time $\tau_3-1$ by the probability that the time $\tau_3$ exactly happens to agree with the time $\tau_1+\tau_2$, which as $\tau_3$ is uniform, is of order $\frac{1}{\log N}$, multiplied with the probability of walk at time  $\tau_1+\tau_2-1$ being at vertex $z$. The reason this final lower bound is not actually very wasteful is that  $z$ has a blue edge, and typically the walk visits a constant number of vertices with blue edges in logarithmic time, which means that unless $\tau_3-1$ agrees with some of these constant number of times, it could not possibly be at $z$. Therefore, it is not unreasonable that insisting that $\tau_3-1$ agrees with one specific such time (namely $\tau_1+\tau_2-1$) when the walk is at a vertex with a blue edge would give a lower bound of the correct order.  


\item {Using \Cref{most_blue_nice}, the lower bound on $|\mathcal{A}_x|$ and $|\mathcal{A}_y|$ that we obtained above, and \Cref{hit_almost_nice_quickly} we see that for sufficiently small values of $\theta$ and sufficiently large values of $C$ we have $\left|\mathcal{A}_x\cap\mathcal{A}_y\cap\mathcal{A}_C\right|\asymp\frac{N}{\log N}$, hence we get that $\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau_1+\tau_2+\tau_3}=y\right)\gtrsim\frac{\deg(y)}{N}$. By definition $\tau_1+\tau_2+\tau_3\le(C_1+C_2+C_3)\log N$. This finishes the proof.}\qedhere
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Combining \Cref{hit_almost_nice_quickly} and \Cref{tauhat_transition_probs} we get that for any $\alpha\in(0,1)$ we have $\mathrm{hit}_{\alpha}\left(\theta\right)\lesssim\log N$ for some $\theta\in(0,1)$. By considering multiple trials, we can extend this for all $\alpha,\theta\in(0,1)$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
From~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{mixing-hitting-large-sets} we know that for any $\alpha\in\left(0,\frac12\right)$ the lazy mixing time is of the same order as
\[t_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\alpha\right):=\quad\max_{x,A:\pi(A)\ge\alpha}\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\tau_A\right].\]
From \Cref{tauhat_transition_probs} we know that for any $x$ and any $A$ we have $\mathbb{P}_{x}\!\left(X_{\tau}\in A,\:\tau\le C\log N\right)\ge\frac{\theta}{N}\sum_{v\in A}\deg(v)-o(1)$, and from \Cref{total_degree} we know that $\frac1N\sum_{v\in A}\deg(v)\asymp\pi(A)$. Using these we get that $\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\tau_A\right]\lesssim\frac1\alpha\log N$ for any $A$ with $\pi(A)\ge\alpha$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
We will show that whp the Cheeger constant satisfies $\Phi^*\lesssim\frac{1}{\log N}$, and then use that $t_\mathrm{rel}^{\mathrm{abs}}\gtrsim\frac{1}{\Phi^*}$.

Let $S=\{1,...,\frac{n}{2}\}\times\mathbb{Z}_n^{d-1}$. Then
\[\Phi^*\quad\le\quad\frac{Q(S,S^c)}{\pi(S)\wedge\pi(S^c)}\quad=\quad\frac{\sum_{x\in S,\:y\in S^c}\1{x\sim y}}{\left(\sum_{v\in S}\deg(v)\right)\wedge\left(\sum_{v\in S^c}\deg(v)\right)}.\]
